The single base of mounted projects (RN-500)​

RN-500 — There's ONE base for mounted projects, it's mounted by identity, and absent means "don't offer the mode"​

BRABO_PROJECTS_BASE is the only folder of the operator's computer that Brabo's containers see. It's mounted by identity ($X:$X) in the api and engine services, which means the path is the SAME on the host and inside both containers.

The identity isn't a style preference. The projects.workspace_path string is typed by the user and shown back to them; with host ≠ container the product would have to choose which of the two to keep, and any choice makes the screen lie to someone. And it's what makes projectScopeRoot (api) and Engine.Actions.Workspace.workspace_dir/2 (engine) remain correct without a single new line of code — the leading-slash discriminator still holds, and the terminal scope of ADR 0055 keeps authorizing exactly the folder the user sees.

Absent is a NORMAL state, not an error. baseDeProjetos() returns null when the variable isn't defined or is empty, and NEVER throws. null travels to the client through GET /workspaces/:workspaceId/projects-base (maintainer, the same minimum as POST .../projects, because it's to decide what that route offers that the value exists) and that's how project creation learns not to offer the Mounted folder mode. Offering a mode the installation doesn't honor produces a project that locks up later, at the first tool of the first agent, far from the screen where the decision was made — it's the same lesson as RN-170.

dentroDaBaseDeProjetos reuses dentroDoEscopo, the same function as the terminal scope, and not a prefix comparison written again: the trap is exactly the one it already solves — /home/voce/brabo2 is not inside /home/voce/brabo, although the string starts the same. The base itself counts as inside; with a null base, nothing is inside.

The base is its OWN variable, never PROJECT_WORKSPACES_HOST_DIR. The three reasons are in the ADR, and the first has data consequences: a managed workspace is named by workspace_dir_name (UNIQUE) and a mounted project is named by the user, so <base>/loja and a container project with workspace_dir_name = loja would land in the SAME physical folder, with init_from_bare! doing git init inside the other's project.

The checkout guard lives in the preflight, and it's the only place where it's possible. pnpm dev refuses to come up when the base overlaps Brabo's checkout, in both directions. The api can't do that check: it compares against process.cwd(), which inside its container is /workspace, and never sees the real path on disk. Without that guard, whoever clones Brabo into $HOME/brabo and points the base there passes all the existing validation and makes the dev agents execute inside the product's own tree — ADR 0055's failure coming in through a door it doesn't watch.

What this RN does NOT do: it doesn't require a mounted project to be inside the base. caminhoDeWorkspaceLocalValido and projectScopeRoot stay intact — that predicate runs on every READ, and a legacy mounted project outside the base would start blowing up when read. The base is a CREATION and CONVERSION rule, and comes in the next RN.

  • Test: apps/api/test/infrastructure/filesystem/project-workspaces-root.spec.ts (describe('baseDeProjetos / dentroDaBaseDeProjetos')) and scripts/dev/base-de-projetos.spec.ts

The base's consent, on the host (RN-511)​

RN-511 — The base is CONSENTED once on the host, sharing is proven by MOUNTING, and without a terminal the step reports instead of consenting​

RN-500 built the base and said what to do when it's missing — projectsBase: null, and the "Mounted folder" mode isn't offered. What was missing was someone asking for it to be configured: nothing in the product did, and the result is that a ready mode became unreachable for whoever installs.

The consent step lives in pnpm bootstrap (Docker › Projects base), proposes $HOME/projetos-brabo, and accepts another typed path. The name isn't a preference: .env.example already uses ~/brabo-projetos as an example of PROJECT_WORKSPACES_HOST_DIR, the root the PRODUCT manages, and proposing the same name for both variables would be walking into the collision that ADR 0141 refused — <base>/loja would land in the same physical folder as a container project whose workspace_dir_name was also loja, and the bootstrap would do git init inside the other's project.

The name is only the dodge; the protection is a mechanism. validarBase refuses any candidate that overlaps — in BOTH directions — Brabo's checkout (the guard RN-500 already had) or PROJECT_WORKSPACES_HOST_DIR (the new rule), besides refusing ~, a relative path, and the root. The refusal applies to the TYPED path, not only to the default; a well-chosen default only avoids the refusal being the first thing the user sees.

Docker Desktop sharing is proven by MOUNTING, never read from settings.json. That file isn't documented, changes between versions and between macOS and Windows, and describes what the user CONFIGURED — not what the daemon will do. It's the same ruler of "a capability is only declared when proven by execution" of ADRs 0041/0042, applied to the host. The proof is a sentinel, and not a bare ls: an empty folder and a non-shared folder produce the same empty listing, so the script writes a file and asks whether the container sees it. Only on macOS and Windows (process.platform); on Linux there's no sharing list, and the check is existence and write. It's the product's SECOND platform guard, symmetric to the first (validarDirDentroDoHomeNoLinux, in the runner): each one restricts only where the restriction means something.

The proof has three outcomes, and they don't collapse: proven; failed (the variable is not written, and the refusal names the path and where to add it); and couldn't prove — no local Docker image to mount —, which writes the variable and says out loud that the proof didn't run, with the command to run it later. "Couldn't look" becoming "everything's fine" is exactly how a non-shared base would reach the user in the form of a container that comes up with an empty folder, far from the screen where the choice was made.

Without a TTY, the step REPORTS and does nothing. The bootstrap.sh menu item runs with stdin coming from /dev/null — on purpose, otherwise anything that reads stdin steals the user's arrow keys — so from there the script can only report, and the output says the command that asks. It's the same design as perguntarUsoDoOllama, which without a terminal applies the default and warns instead of hanging. A consent script that "consents" on its own in a CI pipe is the negation of the word. For the same reason preflight.mjs reports the base's state and never asks: the answer is a path on someone's disk, and there's no default that can be applied silently.

mkdir -p only happens after acceptance and validation — creating a folder from a path that hasn't yet gone through the refusals is creating a folder in any place the process reaches. And an already present value is never overwritten without confirmation.

  • Where: scripts/dev/consentir-base.mjs (the I/O: ask, prove, create, write); scripts/dev/base-de-projetos.mjs:143 (basePadrao), :177 (validarBase), and :208 (exigeProvaDeCompartilhamento) — the pure decision; scripts/dev/env-file.mjs (lerEnv/escreverEnv, extracted from preflight.mjs, which runs await main() at the top and therefore can't be imported); scripts/dev/bootstrap.sh (item 1.6); scripts/dev/preflight.mjs (relatarBaseDeProjetos)

The broker comes up by default in the local compose (RN-512)​

RN-512 — The broker leaves profiles in the LOCAL compose and only there, and DOCKER_GID now gets reported in the preflight​

The broker was born under profiles: ["container-broker"] with a justification that ADR 0130 itself wrote: "giving access to the host's Docker to a process that nothing calls yet would be a posture change for every development machine, in exchange for nothing". Both halves died. "Nothing calls it" is false since ADRs 0133/0134/0136 — the broker has four real callers. And "in exchange for nothing" stopped describing the trade when ADR 0144 made mounted bring up a container THROUGH THE BROKER and ADR 0146 made mounted the local default: with the profile off, the default mode ends in BrokerIndisponivelError.

So it leaves profiles in docker/docker-compose.yml — and only there. In docker/docker-compose.prod.yml the profile STAYS, and the two files start diverging on purpose.

The asymmetry is what the socket means on each side. Whoever runs pnpm dev already has the Docker socket — they're running docker compose, against the host's own daemon —, so the broker receiving it grants nothing the operator doesn't already have. The marginal surface is the broker's own HTTP, which publishes no port, lives on an internal: true network only the api reaches, and compares BRABO_SERVICE_TOKEN in constant time. In production the calculation is the opposite: the socket is a real privilege boundary, the operator isn't the developer, and nothing in this phase changes the default mode of a production installation.

The five containment layers aren't touched. This changes when the broker runs, never what it accepts: it still receives projectId and one of the five operations, still goes to the api to read the Arquiteto's decision, and still has no parameter where one could write privileged, cap_add, network: host, or a free -v. The containment was never the profile.

The environmental consequence, and why it got reported. DOCKER_GID stops mattering only to whoever turned the profile on on purpose — someone who was, by definition, paying attention to it — and starts applying to anyone who runs pnpm dev. The socket is root:docker on the host and the broker's process runs non-root; the compose's group_add is what gives it the group, and the default 999 is the most common and is wrong in several distributions. Getting it wrong doesn't break boot — the broker comes up normally —, it breaks USE: every operation dies with permission denied on the socket, and the symptom appears much later, when someone proposes container_start. That's why preflight.mjs now reports the state on every pnpm dev.

The report has three outcomes, and they don't collapse: matches; diverges (with the origin of the effective value — configurado × default — because the two ask for different instructions); and doesn't apply, when the machine has no docker group. The third isn't an error nor "couldn't": on macOS and Windows Docker Desktop doesn't use a unix group, and in a rootless Docker the socket belongs to the user themselves. Treating the absence as a divergence would accuse half the machines of a defect they don't have — the same care as baseSobrepoeOCheckout, which returns false for an unknown checkout. And it reports, never blocks: pnpm dev comes up the same.

Leaving profiles wasn't enough, and the defect only appeared on the first default startup. The development image prepared pnpm with corepack as root at build time and ran as uid 1000, which doesn't read that cache; without the cache corepack tries to download pnpm at start, and the broker's only network is internal: true — the attempt died with getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN registry.npmjs.org and the container exited with 1, five seconds after coming up. The service also had no healthcheck, so up --wait printed Healthy and the total reset announced "reset completo" with the process dead. While the service was under a profile this never showed up: whoever turned it on on purpose was already watching. The fix takes the registry out of the runtime path — the pnpm install moves to a BUILD step and COREPACK_HOME goes to a directory owned by the runtime uid — and doesn't open the network, which is the first of the five layers above. Since the three node_modules are named volumes mounted over what the image installed, and Docker only seeds an empty volume, docker/broker/entrypoint.sh reconciles the three against a copy kept outside /workspace, stamped with the sha256 of the build's pnpm-lock.yaml — the same stamp that, compared to the tree's lockfile, warns that the image is stale without refusing to come up. The PRODUCTION compose didn't suffer from this: Dockerfile.prod already installed in a build stage, removed corepack from the final image, and already had a HEALTHCHECK. Since AT-360 no image uses corepack (Node 25+ doesn't ship it): pnpm is installed from the registry tarball, checked against a sha512 recorded in the Dockerfile, in /usr/local/bin, and COREPACK_HOME left the dev broker — with the version equal to packageManager's there's no cache to read nor download to attempt at start (measured under --network none).

  • Where: docker/docker-compose.yml (broker service, without profiles, with healthcheck) and docker/docker-compose.prod.yml (with profiles, and the note that prevents uniformizing the two); docker/broker/Dockerfile (pnpm pinned by sha512, the build-time pnpm install, and the copy in /opt/broker-deps); docker/broker/entrypoint.sh (the reconciliation of the three volumes and the lockfile warning); scripts/dev/docker-gid.mjs (avaliarDockerGid, mensagemDoDockerGid, GID_PADRAO_DO_COMPOSE — the pure decision); scripts/dev/preflight.mjs (relatarDockerGid, gidDoGrupoDocker)

The base decides what project creation offers (RN-513)​

RN-513 — With a consented base, mounted is preselected with <base>/<slug> suggested; without a base, or without knowing, it isn't offered​

Revised by RN-573 (ADR 0161): the preselection of mounted now ALSO requires the container broker confirmed. With a base and no broker (the installation from a Release), runner is preselected and container/mounted stay inert with the reason in text; with the broker unknown, container stays selected. The rest of this rule holds as is.

Two halves of this rule were already rules and had never reached the client. "Don't offer the mode without a base" is RN-500; "suggest <base>/<slug>" is RN-501, and ADR 0142 postponed disk validation precisely so that the wizard could propose a folder that doesn't exist yet. Until now, GET /workspaces/:workspaceId/projects-base had no caller at all in the web, and the "Mounted folder" card was offered unconditionally — in an installation without BRABO_PROJECTS_BASE, choosing the mode ended in a 400 refusal from the api after the person had chosen, typed the path, and reached the end of the wizard.

What's new is the preselection: with a configured base, mounted is born selected. It revises the default of ADR 0072 (where container is "the normal one" and the local mode is an escape hatch) and revises it only for the local installation, where the base was consented by a human on the host (RN-511). The project_execution_mode enum doesn't change, no new mode is born, and mode conversion (ADR 0111) isn't touched.

The query is born with the wizard, not with the step. The "Where the code will live" step is the fifth; a useQuery mounted only there would make the card appear flickering after the person was already looking at the screen.

Unknown doesn't become an offer. While the answer hasn't arrived, and also when the query fails (403, network, api down), the card doesn't appear and container stays selected. A failure isn't permission to offer a mode whose precondition couldn't be confirmed: it's the same ruler as RN-088/RN-468 — the product doesn't collapse "don't know" with "doesn't have" — and that of ADRs 0041/0042, where a capability is only declared when proven.

The preselection never overrides a human choice. The base arrives over the network, always AFTER the first render. The screen keeps the user's choice separate from the current mode (modoDeWorkspaceEscolhido × modoDeWorkspace), and the preselection only holds while nobody has touched the cards — swapping the mode under the hand of whoever already clicked is a defect, not a convenience.

The suggestion never clobbers what was typed. <base>/<slug> comes in in two cases and only in them: an empty field with nothing suggested yet, or a field containing exactly this screen's previous suggestion (the name changed in the details step, and the suggestion follows). Anything else — including the empty field after the user deleted the suggestion — stays as it is. An empty slug (adoption, where the name comes from the provider) doesn't become an invented segment: the field stays empty, and canAdvanceFromWorkspace holds the step. The field is editable the whole time; the preselection didn't relax any advance ruler.

And the mode's warning stopped lying. The previous text predated ADR 0141: it said the path was free and that it would only work if the user mounted it. Today there are two states, and they're the two the backend has — under the base, a neutral note (creation passes, and the folder doesn't even need to exist: the Infra creates it when bringing up the container, RN-501); outside the base, a warning saying that the api refuses creation (400, in resolverWorkspacePath) and naming the base, instead of telling you to go look for the variable. An empty field isn't "outside the base": there's no path for the api to refuse yet, and alarming before the person types would be the screen asserting about what it doesn't have. The comparison is by segment, never a raw startsWith — /base-outra isn't inside /base —, mirroring the api's dentroDoEscopo.

The mounted folder is born when the container comes up (RN-501)​

RN-501 — mounted validates only the LEXICON and the base at creation; the folder is MATERIALIZED later, by whoever has authority over the disk​

Creating a mounted project stopped touching disk. It requires two things, and both are lexical:

  1. the same predicate runner already used (caminhoDeWorkspaceLocalValido) — absolute, no .., outside the root and system folders, not overlapping Brabo's checkout (RN-422/RN-423);
  2. being inside BRABO_PROJECTS_BASE (RN-500), which is the only folder of the computer the api's and the engine's containers see.

The project is born with workspaceVerifiedAt: null, exactly like a runner.

Why postpone. The requirement is the product owner's and it's literal: "if it's a Mounted folder, the bind-mount must be created AFTER the architect's decision". Disk validation ran at CREATION, which is the first screen of the flow, and the Arquiteto's decision happens many sessions later — requiring the folder ready at creation is requiring it before any decision exists. And it's what prevented mounted from being a first-class choice: a path SUGGESTED by the wizard (<base>/<slug>) is, by construction, a path that doesn't exist yet.

The difference between mounted and runner was never what counts as a valid path — it's when and who confirms the disk. In runner it's the CLI connecting; in mounted it's the materialization.

Without a configured base, the MODE isn't available. The refusal says so, with the variable's name and what the operator needs to do — it never pretends the path was what was wrong. Outside the base, the refusal names the base and suggests <base>/<the name the person asked for>, never the bare base, which would teach putting the project at the root of all of them. Both messages come from ONE source (motivoDeForaDaBaseDeProjetos), because the two doors that apply the rule — creation/conversion and materialization — refuse for the same reason.

The materialization (materializarWorkspaceMontado) is mkdir -p plus the usual three disk questions (does it exist? is it a folder? can it be written?), with the refusal for being outside the base before the mkdir — otherwise a path written outside the product would make the api create a folder anywhere it reaches. Two callers:

  • ExecuteContainerStartUseCase — the normal one. When the Infra brings up the container, the folder is created, proven writable, and workspace_verified_at is stamped by the SAME path ConfirmProjectWorkspaceUseCase uses. Failing is a NAMED failed, never a throw nor a 500 — the same discipline as BrokerIndisponivelError/RunnerNaoConectadoError —, and the lifecycle does not get marked provisioning: marking it and only then finding out that it can't write would leave project_containers asserting a state that never existed. The message names the variable, the path, the probable cause (the folder's owner on the host; the images run non-root, ADR 0024), and the next step ("approve container_start again").
  • ConvertProjectExecutionModeUseCase — the exception, declared. Conversion has no container step to hang the work on, and right after it MOVES permissions.json to permissionsFilePath(localNova), which in mounted is the user's folder. Moving a file into a nonexistent folder fails, so here mkdir-at-decision is right — before the transaction, so the refusal doesn't leave a transaction open, and becoming a 400.

What this RN does NOT do, and it's the easiest regression to cause. The base rule does not go into caminhoDeWorkspaceLocalValido. That predicate runs on EVERY READ, through projectScopeRoot (terminal scope, permissions.json, Code tab), and a LEGACY mounted project — created when the bind-mount was one compose line per project, therefore outside the base — would start blowing up with LocalizacaoDeProjetoInvalidaError when simply read. The base is a creation and conversion rule; the lexicon is forever.

No migration, and the database CHECK stays intact. mounted keeps writing a NON-null workspace_path, so (execution_mode <> 'container') = (workspace_path IS NOT NULL) remains satisfied. Postponing verification never touches the pairing invariant.

Declared consequence: between creating the project and bringing up the container, workspace_path points to a folder that may not exist. Nothing breaks (projectScopeRoot is lexical; permissions.json degrades to EMPTY_PERMISSIONS_FILE, which is require_approval on everything), but the screen needs to SAY so — a screen that shows a path without saying it doesn't exist yet is a screen asserting what it doesn't know.

A mounted project brings up a container through the BROKER (RN-503)​

RN-503 — A mounted project brings up a container through the BROKER, and what crosses the network is a discriminated locator — never an absolute path​

A project in Mounted folder mode couldn't get any container until now, and for two independent blocks: ExecuteContainerStartUseCase sent every mode other than container to the RUNNER (which requires a connected brabo-runner), and the broker refused at the source any mode that wasn't container, with ModoDeExecucaoNaoSuportadoError.

Both existed for the same reason of GEOMETRY, not because of the mode's name: the folder of a mounted project was in an arbitrary place on the operator's disk, which the server's Docker daemon had no reason to see. ADR 0141 (RN-500) changed that geometry — every mounted project now lives under one base mounted by identity —, and that's what, and only what, this rule harvests.

The branching is now by DESTINATION, not by mode. container and mounted go to the BROKER; only runner goes to the runner, because its folder remains on a machine this server doesn't reach (ADR 0137). The same holds for the three lifecycle actions — container_start, container_stop, and container_remove: they HAVE to change together, otherwise a mounted project's container comes up on the server and the request to stop goes looking for it on the user's machine, leaving up, with no way to stop it, what is up.

ADR 0130's invariant doesn't move: no absolute path crosses the network. The broker is root-equivalent on the host and COMPOSES the -v from ITS roots; if the api sent /home/voce/brabo/loja, the bind-mount's containment would come to depend on the api being correct, which is exactly the dependency the broker exists not to have. What changes is that now there are TWO roots on the other side, so the spec needs to SAY against which of them the relative piece applies — and it says so, in a discriminated locator:

localizacao.tiposegmentbroker root
gerenciadaworkspace_dir_name (RN-109)PROJECT_WORKSPACES_HOST_ROOT
montadathe RELATIVE path under the baseBRABO_PROJECTS_HOST_BASE
indisponivel— (there's a motivo)none

Three states and not two, because the third really exists and has two different fixes: a runner project (the folder is on another machine — the fix is the runner, on the other side) and a LEGACY mounted project created outside the base (the fix is moving the folder). Collapsing them into a null would make the same absence send whoever operates to the wrong place. The folder that IS the base itself also falls here, and doesn't become an empty segment: <raiz>/ would mount the whole base — the folder of ALL mounted projects — inside the container of a single one.

The lack of one root is never supplied by the other. Without BRABO_PROJECTS_HOST_BASE, a mounted project's start refuses naming the variable (BaseDeProjetosNaoConfiguradaError, origin infra, 503) and doesn't touch any container — the same mold as RaizDeWorkspacesNaoConfiguradaError. Falling to the other root by omission would be the worst possible outcome: the managed root is named by workspace_dir_name and the base is named by the user, so the same name points to different folders and the container would come up with ANOTHER project's folder, with nothing indicating why. For the same reason, the list of modes the broker serves is an ALLOWLIST: a new mode in the enum is born refused, with a message, instead of accepted by omission.

The composition still goes through three barriers, not one. The api refuses what isn't under the base (segmentoSobABaseDeProjetos); the broker refuses a segment that isn't relative (segmentoDeProjetoValidado — .., absolute, empty, double slash, NUL); and the concatenation's result still goes through raizDeProjetoValidada before becoming a -v. Validating the segment and not validating the concatenation would be trusting string arithmetic.

mounted ELECTS the image, like container — it doesn't read the current one like the runner. It isn't aesthetic symmetry: it's the only design that works. The broker composes from artifact.project_image, going to FETCH it from the api. An Infra election that wasn't recorded in that artifact would be inert — the container would come up with the image the Arquiteto decided, the payload the human approved would say another, and nothing in the record would expose the difference. The runner's path can read the current one precisely because there the api SENDS the spec's fields through the channel; there the artifact isn't the source the other side consults.

What this rule does NOT do: it materializes no folder — whoever creates the folder of the mounted project is RN-501, in the SAME use case and before this branching, precisely because the server's daemon needs the folder to exist to mount it. It also doesn't touch the image gate (RN-105 already applies to the three modes since RN-494) and doesn't change who PROPOSES container_start — the Infra Lead can still propose for a project with no connected runner and no decided image, the gap declared since RN-494.

The folder browser served by the api (RN-504)​

RN-504 — The folder browser is scoped to the projects base and NEVER leaves it​

GET /workspaces/:workspaceId/project-folders lists the subfolders of a path, and exists because the project creation wizard loses, at once, BOTH "browse folder" mechanisms it had: FolderBrowserModal navigated through the runner's websocket (fs_list_dir/fs_home_dir) and RunnerOnboardingPanel used showDirectoryPicker, which returns a browser handle and never an absolute path. Without a runner, the browser has no way to list any filesystem — and it's an absolute path that projects.workspace_path keeps.

The containment is ONE, and it's hard. path is optional and omitted means the base (baseDeProjetos()); every provided path has to satisfy dentroDaBaseDeProjetos (RN-500), which reuses dentroDoEscopo — the same function as ADR 0055's terminal scope — and that's why it catches the prefix trap: /home/voce/brabo2 is not inside /home/voce/brabo, although the string starts the same. .. and . are refused instead of resolved, for the same reason as caminhoDeWorkspaceLocalValido: resolving would accept that the path read isn't the path requested.

Leaving the base is 400, and not 403. 403 would say "you don't have permission to see this" and would suggest another role would see it — that's not the case. There's no role that navigates outside the base, because outside the base isn't a more privileged area, it's an area this route simply doesn't address. The request is MALFORMED.

The ceilings are a contract, not an implementation detail: only directories in entries; at most 500, sorted before the cut (otherwise "the first 500" would be the order the filesystem returned, which changes between machines); no recursion; entries starting with . left out; and symlinks reported, never descended — readdirSync(withFileTypes) has lstat semantics, so a link pointing outside the base isn't an exit door. What's left out is COUNTED (arquivos, simbolicos, truncado): without that a folder full of code would come back as an empty list and the screen would say "empty folder", asserting about what it didn't read (RN-180).

There's no POST. Creating a folder belongs to the mounted workspace's materialization, at the moment the container comes up — never to the picker.

The minimum is maintainer, the same as POST .../projects and .../projects-base, and by the same reasoning one step further: projects-base reveals ONE path of the operator's machine, this route reveals the TOPOLOGY below it. Inheriting the viewer of the neighboring routes because they're neighbors is the defect RN-102 names — the minimum is the ENDPOINT's, never the section's. workspaceId doesn't enter the calculation: the base belongs to the INSTALLATION, and it's in the route because it's what gives scope to RolesGuard.

On the client, the transport becomes one of the TWO implementations of the FsBrowser interface (apps/web/src/lib/fs-browser.ts): criarFsBrowserViaApi (new) and connectFsBrowserChannel (the runner's channel, retyped). FolderBrowserModal chooses by origem: { tipo: 'api'; workspaceId } | { tipo: 'runner'; projectId } — a discriminated union, and not two optional props, because "neither of the two" and "both" would be representable states the component would have to handle at runtime. The transport via runner is left with no caller in the web from here on, and stays in the repository by the product owner's declared decision (the runner leaves the interface, the binary keeps being refined); the protocol in apps/runner/src/channel.ts isn't touched in any way.

RN-509 — A module Dev Agent's "Always allow" scopes to agent_autonomy, PER AGENT — no longer the whole project's permissions.json​

ApproveAlwaysActionUseCase always wrote to permissions.json/allow — WHOLE PROJECT scope, shared by any actor. That meant "always allowing" a command for dev-checkout released the SAME command for dev-auth, for dev-lead, and for any future agent of the project: the intent of whoever clicked ("I trust THIS agent with THIS") had no way to be expressed — only "I trust anyone with this" existed.

The write now branches by ACTOR, inside the SAME use case (not a new one — duplicating the two absolute-ceiling guards for out-of-scope terminal/git_push/sudo and for container_remove in two places would be the same defect RN-418/RN-495 already exist to avoid):

  • An agent actor whose id is dev-<modulo> (ADR 0053/PHASE 14d — the DYNAMIC dev area, one agent per module_map module): writes to agent_autonomy(projectId, agentId, actionType) = auto_approve, through the SAME AgentAutonomyRepository.upsert that activate-execution.use-case.ts already calls to seed the three git actions per module. permissions.json stays untouched.
  • Any other actor — user, system, an agent agent that isn't a module dev, and dev-lead — keeps going to the usual permissions.json/allow, whole-project scope, exactly as before.

dev-lead is the exception that needs its own name. ehDevDeModulo (agent-areas.ts) is PURE agentId.startsWith('dev-'), on purpose — and that classifies dev-lead as true. What excludes the lead from its own area is ehMembroDe, not ehDevDeModulo alone ("the lead isn't a member of its own area" holds for any area — duplicating the exclusion inside the predicate left both copies unreachable by tests, a finding recorded in the comment of agent-areas.ts itself). That's why the branch uses ehDevDeModulo(actor.id) && actor.id !== DEV_LEAD: without the second term, "always allow" clicked on a dev-lead action would write module autonomy under the LEAD's agentId by accident — an agent that isn't a member of dev, has no module, and that the area never looks at via agent_area_members.

The two absolute ceilings of decide.ts keep running BEFORE the branch, without changing order. Terminal with a git external effect (git push, gh pr create) or privileged (sudo/doas) — RN-106/RN-418 — and container_remove — RN-495 — keep refusing the WHOLE click (400, the action not even approved), for ANY actor, before the project is even fetched. Scoping the write per agent isn't a second door to the same ceiling: the two refusal ifs stay where they were, and the new branch comes after.

The permission.granted event carries one payload OR the other, never one pretending to be the other. { pattern } remains the format of the permissions.json path (the text pattern written to the file); the new path emits { agentId, actionType } — there's no "pattern" at all to show when the write is a table row keyed by agent.

No data migration. Old "always allow" entries written for a module dev in permissions.json, from before this rule existed, stay there exactly as they were — they just no longer receive MORE entries of that kind from then on. A conscious decision by the product owner, not a forgotten gap.

The conversational agents' decision artifact (RN-505)​

RN-505 — decision_record reuses the GENERIC pattern of emit_artifact, not the dedicated one​

A conversational agent that makes a relevant decision in a conversation (why it chose X and not Y, what it considered, what it accepted to lose) records it with emit_artifact and type: decision_record — a payload with context, options (list), choice, and consequences, the four mandatory keys in Engine.Harness.ArtifactSchemas (artifact_schemas.ex:82), tool-emittable since it entered @tool_emittable (artifact_schemas.ex:98). No cross validation on purpose: choice doesn't need to match an item of options — free text is more robust, and the generic schema only validates key presence (the same ruler as note/business_rule).

Why reuse the GENERIC pattern instead of the dedicated one. artifact.project_image and artifact.c4_diagram (neighboring RNs of this one) are VERSIONED artifacts — each emission replaces the previous one as "current", with its own HTTP read route and a dedicated TypeScript schema in the api. A decision isn't like that: it's an append-only record by nature, not a "current" that gets replaced — the same reasoning that already holds for note/business_rule. Paying the price of the dedicated pattern (TS schema, versioning, new route) for a log that only needs to exist and be searchable in the session's event log would cost structure the decision doesn't ask for.

Declared distinction from open_adr_pr (only the Arquiteto has it). The two COEXIST, with different purposes: decision_record is for EVERY relevant decision of any of the six conversational agents, with no friction at all — it never commits a file, never opens a PR, never waits for human approval. open_adr_pr is for when the decision is big enough to become a real DOCUMENT in docs/adr/*.md, with a real PR and mandatory human approval. A project can have ten decision_record and zero ADR in one session — the second isn't the "serious" version of the first, it's another tool for another scale of decision.

Wiring in the five conversational agents that didn't have emit_artifact yet — PO (po_server.ex:115), Arquiteto (arquiteto_server.ex:103), Dev Lead (dev_lead_server.ex:153), UX Designer (ux_designer_server.ex:94), and Staff (staff_server.ex:94); the Criativo already had the tool since Phase 3b, it only gained the new type (it's the shared known/0 that decides, with no change to CriativoServer). In each one, the common run_tool/3 gained the clause "emit_artifact" -> EmitArtifact.run/2 (e.g. po_server.ex:279) — with no special handling: unlike propose_execution_plan/ assess_implementability in the Dev Lead (which suspend the turn waiting for approval, ADR 0086), emit_artifact never returns {:pending, _}, so it enters the common dispatch without needing the reduce_while those two tools require. And the five gained the SAME sentence in system_prompt/1 (e.g. po_server.ex:463) explaining when to use type: decision_record — outside the identity text (Engine.Harness.Agents) because it isn't about WHO the agent is, it's an operational instruction about a tool.

Out of scope, declared. Execution agents (QA, SecOps, module Dev Agent) run on ToolLoop, with no harness common to the six conversational ones — they're left out of this slice, with their own per-module investigation before extending. Tying it to Front 1 of the same plan (the Infra Lead's dispatch emitting a server-emitted decision_record when it proposes bringing up a container via runner) is also left out: it depends on a tool (propose_container_start_via_runner) another PR is creating in parallel — see the TODO in this change's PR.

RN-507 — Docker becomes a real prerequisite of runner mode: the THREE execution modes require the SAME predicate​

Until now, Engine.Actions.TerminalExecutor.decisao_de_execucao/1 checked only TWO preconditions to route the terminal to an execution_mode: runner project — workspace CONFIRMED and runner CONNECTED now — and routed unconditionally as soon as both matched, without checking whether there was a REGISTERED running container (Engine.Containers.ProjectContainerLifecycle.running?/1), the same predicate container/mounted had already required since RN-502 (ADR 0143). The runner on the other side decided on its own whether the command ran inside the container it brought up (ADR 0137) or fell to the bare HOST — and without Docker up on the user's machine, it always fell to the host, silently: the isolation ADR 0134 sought to create for container never applied to runner.

The fix unifies the three modes under the SAME question. runner gains a THIRD precondition, in the same order as the other two: verified → connected → running container. The three named refusals (workspace not verified, runner disconnected, no container) live today in Engine.Runners.RunnerReadiness — extracted because a SECOND consumer was born in the same PR (Engine.Actions.Workspace.RunnerGit, below): "they aren't two derivations, it's this function with two consumers", the same reasoning as the moduledoc of ProjectContainerLifecycle.

The dev agent's worktree materialization changes mechanism, not result. Engine.Actions.Workspace.ensure!/4 tried LOCAL File.mkdir_p!/ System.cmd("git", ...) against the HOST path, even in runner mode — the gap RN-478 recorded and left OPEN on purpose ("the dev agent's working tree has nowhere to be born", since the engine's process has no bind-mount at all for a folder that lives on the user's machine). The fix isn't "improve the error message" again: ensure!/4 now forks by execution_mode — LOCAL for container/mounted (unchanged: mounted already sees its folder via BRABO_PROJECTS_BASE, a bind-mount by identity in the engine since ADR 0141), via Engine.Actions.Workspace. RunnerGit for runner. RunnerGit does git init/remote add/fetch/ checkout (and the equivalents of File.dir?/ls/rm_rf that Engine.Dev.WorktreeManager needs) as NORMAL shell commands, delivered through the SAME Phoenix channel that already executes approved terminal commands (Engine.Runners.RunnerRouter.exec/5) — never a new mechanism, and always after RunnerReadiness.verificar/1 confirms the three preconditions (it raises with a named message before attempting any I/O, never a blind exec). Engine.Dev.WorktreeManager (create/3, remove/2, list/1, cleanup_orphans/2) forks by the same criterion.

The periodic cleanup job SKIPS silently, never fails. Engine.Dev.WorktreeCleanup.run/0 swept File.dir?(work_dir) to decide whether to prune — always false for runner (the path is the HOST's, the engine doesn't see it), so runner was never really pruned nor tested through that path. The gate becomes by MODE: File.dir? stays for container/mounted; for runner, RunnerReadiness.pronto?/1 decides — with no runner connected or no running container NOW, the project is skipped IN THIS round ("can't know now", never an error, never a worktree treated as an orphan by mistake), and Enum.each/2 continues to the following projects without any exception crossing it.

The exec/exec_result protocol gains a NEW field: env (ADR 0056). The authenticated git fetch of RunnerGit needs the provider's credential — which can only travel in the child process's ENVIRONMENT (never argv, never .git/config, the same discipline as the local Engine.Actions.GitAuth). Since the child process is now born on the user's machine, the env field (optional, Record<string,string>) enters the payload that RunnerRouter.exec/5 dispatches — present only when there's a real credential (the local provider never carries it). On the runner's side: apps/runner/src/exec.ts MERGES (never replaces) opts.env on top of process.env before the spawn — an env defined without merge would discard PATH and break the resolution of the git/sh binary itself. apps/runner/src/index.ts passes msg.env only to the HOST path (executarComando) — the container (docker exec, via packages/docker-port) didn't gain env support (out of scope of this delivery: the port's exec operation still lacks that field, on purpose, ADR 0130). No runner log prints env anywhere — audited by grep, console.log/console.warn/console.error keep citing only ref/command/cwd/exitCode.

RN-508 — container_start_via_runner: a second action type to bring up the container, exclusive to runner, and the Infra Lead refuses blind proposals BEFORE proposing​

container_start (ADR 0130/0133) requires imagem/network/resources/ rationale — the Infra ELECTS a candidate from the Arquiteto's routing. Until this delivery, the same action type also served execution_mode: runner (ExecuteContainerStartUseCase.executeViaRunner), but the runner's path NEVER read any of those four fields: the image that comes up is the one already DECIDED (there's no routing to elect against, because the broker never reaches a runner project's folder). Asking for 4 fields the dispatch always discarded is the defect that motivates a separate ACTION being born instead of a "smart" container_start branching by mode.

container_start_via_runner only has rationale (optional). The same caliber as container_start (maintainer, require_approval by default, never seeded in auto-approval, configurable in permissions.json like the other three container actions — it doesn't enter the absolute ceiling of container_remove). ExecuteContainerStartUseCase loses the whole runner branch (executeViaRunner, ApiToEngineClient/ObterSpecDeContainerUseCase leave the constructor) — it becomes exclusive to container/mounted, both through the BROKER (RN-503). The extracted code becomes ExecuteContainerStartViaRunnerUseCase, a sibling file. The lifecycle dance (provisioning -> running) the two paths shared by copy becomes SubirCicloDeVidaDoContainerUseCase (apps/api/.../containers/) — extracted so as not to duplicate the state machine's rationale in the two files.

The Infra Lead queries LOCALLY, without HTTP, before proposing. The new tool (Engine.Infra.Tools.ProposeContainerStartViaRunner) is intercepted by Engine.Infra.InfraLeadServer.dispatch_calls/2, which reads Project.get/1 (execution_mode) and Engine.Runners.Registry.connected?/1 (runner connected) — BOTH reads are already local, in the same BEAM process — BEFORE calling propose_action. It refuses with a NAMED reason (never proposes blindly) when the project is in container (use propose_container_start), in mounted (likewise, since RN-503), or in runner with no runner connected now. This gap — "proposing without knowing whether it'll work" — is the SAME one propose_container_start has had since RN-494, declared and accepted for that tool (touching the Infra Lead's prompt/instruction would be outside the API/domain scope); the NEW tool is born without it, because it's born knowing how to refuse.

The specification the api composes is the one the runner VALIDATES, and that is now proven. EspecificacaoDeContainerParaRunner is the fields of EntradaDeEspecificacao (packages/docker-port) minus raizDoProjeto, which only the runner knows — TEN, not nine. It was born with nine, without projectId, and the consequence was that this path NEVER brought up any container since it existed: the engine passes the map on opaquely, the runner hands it to especificacaoValidada, which requires projectId as non-empty text, and the action ended failed with "especificação de container recusada em projectId: esperava texto não vazio, recebi undefined" — and from there the CORRECT block of RN-507/RN-502 did the rest, with no dev agent claiming a task. The data always existed (SpecDeContainer.projectId, the same one the BROKER receives through GET .../container-spec, and that's why only runner mode broke); it just wasn't copied. Three green suites didn't catch it because each one built its own fixture: the use case's test asserted what it itself expected, the runner's built a fixture WITH projectId, and the engine doesn't look at the map. What is now guaranteed is the CHAIN — the payload ExecuteContainerStartViaRunnerUseCase composes, going through the real especificacaoValidada —, and the test also locks the set of fields: raizDoProjeto is the only one the api doesn't send, so a new field on one side without the other fails.

The local agent's join stops being mute (RN-514)​

RN-514 — The runner DECLARES what it can do on join, the server GRANTS the intersection in socket.assigns, and a message without the capability is REFUSED instead of vanishing​

Until now the join of the terminal:<projectId> channel was mute on both sides: the runner sent socket.channel(\terminal:${projectId}`, {}) and the server literally ignored them (def join("terminal:" <> project_id, _params, socket)). The whole identity came from the ticket — the role (:runner/:web) comes from the kind` —, and the server had no way of knowing whether the binary on the other side was from a version that understands a new message.

The defect this produces is the worst possible one, and it is what this rule closes: the message arrives, the handler does not exist on the other side, and nothing happens — no error, no log, nobody knowing that the function never ran.

Three capabilities, and only what the runner can do is declared. The server's vocabulary is exec (approved command, ADR 0104), pty (interactive terminal, ADR 0103) and espelho (copying the work to a folder outside the mounted base). The runner declares exec and pty, and espelho is left out on purpose: declaring what is not implemented is exactly the defect the negotiation exists to prevent — the server would grant it, deliver the message, and it would vanish just the same. espelho is born only as a name in the vocabulary, with no behavior at all; whoever implements it is session 6 of PHASE 28.

Absence of params is the LEGACY, and that is a fact — not benevolence. Every binary prior to this change sends empty params, and every binary prior to this change can do exec and pty: they are the two functions the runner was born with. Granting {exec, pty} to whoever declares nothing is reading correctly the only thing that binary could have said. The opposite would make every installed runner stop connecting, which is a change requiring operator action before deploy — breaking/ and MAJOR, by the repository's convention, and that is not what this delivery is. Absent params, absent capacidades, an empty list and a value that is not a list all fall into the legacy: they are the shapes that "this binary cannot declare anything" takes on the network path.

Unknown is IGNORED, never a reason for refusal. The granted set is the intersection of what was declared with the vocabulary that this server knows — a runner NEWER than the engine has to be able to connect. Declaring only unknown names, however, is an empty declaration, not legacy: whoever can declare said what it can do.

What each mode REQUIRES. runner requires exec — it is literally what makes the mode work, and without it the TerminalExecutor would route an approved command to a binary that does not execute it, with the failure showing up as a timeout instead of a refusal. container and mounted require nothing (the runner is not even their execution path). Nothing requires espelho yet — the refusal mechanism is born implemented and tested, and does not fire in practice today. That is the design, not a pending item. A mode that could not be read (nonexistent project, malformed id, failed query) requires nothing: refusing on an unconfirmed precondition would be collapsing "I don't know" with "it doesn't have" (RN-088).

The granted set lives in socket.assigns, never in a table. A capability is a property of that connection — a table could claim that a runner knows something the process connected now does not. It is the same reasoning that makes the :global entry of Engine.Runners.Registry die together with the pid. Only the :runner role receives a set: the :web socket does not get :capacidades and no capability check applies to it — the tab executes nothing, it asks.

A join refusal names the one missing. {:error, %{reason: ...}} saying which capability the project requires and that the binary needs to be updated. The refusal is fatal on the runner side, with no retry (JoinRecusadoError, behavior that already existed and did not change) — that is why it is the only chance to explain, and "refused" without the name of what is missing would force guessing. The check happens before Registry.register/2: registering and then refusing would leave the Registry asserting a runner that did not get in.

And the half that delivers value today: a message without the granted capability is REFUSED with a named reply, never swallowed. exec to a runner without exec answers the caller in the same exec_result format that the runner would send (exitCode 126 — "found, but not executable" —, the cause in output), instead of leaving the RunnerRouter blocked until the receive ... after and the user seeing a timeout in place of the cause. pty_* to a runner without pty is not relayed, and the originating :web receives a named pty_error, through the same filtered broadcast the runner would use to report a PTY error — without it the tab would stay "loading" forever, the defect that the whereis of handle_in("pty_open", ...) had already closed for the "no runner" case. Since the legacy has both capabilities, nothing changes for anyone today.

This is not a security boundary. A capability is a protocol negotiation; what authorizes is still the single-use ticket (RN-108) and the proposed_action pipeline. What the runner gains by declaring is that messages of that type are delivered to it, never permission for anything.

The mirror destination is per project (RN-515)​

RN-515 — The mirror destination is declared PER PROJECT and is never global; null is the normal state; and the api validates ONLY the lexicon, saying it is only the lexicon​

The espelho capability (RN-514, ADR 0147) copies the agents' work to a user folder outside the mounted base — which is the reason it exists, because a bind mount does not cross a network nor reach a path outside what was mounted. This rule decides where that destination lives and how the user declares it; it does not copy any file.

PER PROJECT, never global. The destination is the projects.mirror_path column and the project's mirrorPath field, written by PUT /projects/:projectId/mirror-path (maintainer, the same minimum as execution-mode and projects-base: the route speaks of a path on the operator's computer). Never a global setting in the runner, never an environment variable: a global destination would make project B's artifact land in project A's folder, and the user would find that out through the content, not through an error (ADR 0147, point 4).

null is the NORMAL state, not a pending item. The column is nullable and is born null; a project without a mirror is the majority, and the product never picks a destination on its own. Clearing is {"mirrorPath": null} — the key is mandatory, and omitting it is 400: a body that omits the field would be indistinguishable from "clear", and clearing silently is precisely the defect. Clearing always works, even in a container project, otherwise a converted row would be stuck in the state the rule forbids.

Only the LEXICON, and the api SAYS it is only the lexicon. The api does not see the machine where the destination will exist — it is the situation of the runner mode (RN-423), not that of mounted, where the folder ends up inside the base the api actually reaches. It reuses caminhoDeWorkspaceLocalValido, the same predicate as creation and conversion (absolute, no ../., never the root nor a system folder, never overlapping the Brabo checkout), instead of a fourth copy of the same rule — and it does not require BRABO_PROJECTS_BASE, because the mirror destination is by definition the folder the base does not cover. The refusal message declares that the disk was not verified and who verifies it.

The two directions of the same loop. A destination inside the workspacePath and a destination that contains the workspacePath are the same refusal seen from two sides (ADR 0147, point 2): writing the mirror inside the source makes the mirror copy itself, and a source inside the destination nests the copy on every round. Refusing one and allowing the other would be closing the door and leaving the window open. The comparison is by SEGMENT (dentroDoEscopo), never raw startsWith: /base-outra is not inside /base, and refusing it would penalize a perfectly legitimate sibling folder.

This is the LEXICAL half of the guard, and only it. The other is realpath, and it belongs to the RUNNER (espelho-guard.ts, ADR 0147 point 2), on the machine where both paths really exist. A symlink in any segment of the destination pointing back to the source passes through here unseen — the api has no disk on which to resolve it. The api did not guarantee the loop; it prevented the WRITTEN loop.

container is refused, and the refusal is NAMED. The source of a container project is a managed volume on the server, and whoever would copy is a process on the user's machine, which does not see it. Accepting and never copying would be worse than refusing, because it would look configured. mounted and runner can. For the same reason, converting the mode ZEROES the destination (RN-447..450): in container it could not exist, and even between mounted and runner the conversion MOVES the source against which both directions of the loop were validated.

The value comes back in every project read (ProjectResponseDto.mirrorPath), so the mirror implementation and the status screen do not need a new route. There is no dedicated read endpoint.

And it is NOT a proposed_action. Writing the mirror is configuration the user declared, not an agent asking to act — ADR 0147 is explicit about it, and syncing via a terminal command would fall into the scope of ADR 0055 and become a queue of routine approvals.

The mirror copies the work to the user's folder (RN-516)​

RN-516 — The mirror destination travels in the join GRANT, the mirror copies the git list in one direction only and never deletes, and the trigger is a named moment — never a watcher​

Half B of session 6 of PHASE 28: the espelho capability (RN-514, ADR 0147) comes to EXIST. RN-515 decided where the destination lives and did not copy any file; this one decides how it reaches the local agent, what is copied and when.

The destination travels in the join grant, never in runner configuration. The join reply of the terminal:<projectId> channel is no longer empty for the :runner role: when the project has a declared destination (projects.mirror_path) and the espelho capability was granted, it carries %{espelho: %{destino: "<caminho>"}}. The runner keeps this in estado.destinoDoEspelho, which dies with the connection, and refuses mirror_sync for a destination not granted to it on that connection (ADR 0147, point 4). Never an environment variable, never a local file: a global destination would make project B's artifact land in project A's folder, and the user would find that out through the content, not through an error.

A declared consequence, and it is the price: changing the destination with the runner connected requires reconnecting it. The grant belongs to the join, and a new destination arriving through another door would be exactly the global configuration the rule refuses.

A non-null mirror_path now REQUIRES the capability. It does not enter the map by execution_mode — what requires it is a project DATUM, not the mode (and mounted and runner can have a destination while container cannot). This is the first REAL case of the refusal mechanism RN-514 left implemented and never firing: a brabo-runner older than this version connected to a project with a destination stops connecting, with a named refusal (JoinRecusadoError, fatal and with no retry). It is opt-in — it only happens where someone configured a destination — and the cost is declared in ADR 0147 itself.

The THREE refusals of the guard, and the realpath pass is not redundant. apps/runner/src/espelho-guard.ts is a sibling of guard.ts, not an extension of it: it reuses semBarraFinal/dentroDoEscopo/realpathMaisProximo and the double lexical-then-realpath pass of validarCwdDentroDaRaiz, and inherits in writing the same TOCTOU caveat — it is best-effort, not a security boundary. It refuses (1) a symlink escaping the destination, (2) a destination that contains the workspace and (3) a destination inside the workspace; (2) and (3) are the same loop in opposite directions, and with the identity bind of ADR 0141 writing the mirror inside the source makes the mirror copy itself. The api already refused the lexical half (RN-515) and says, in the code itself, that it is only the lexicon — it has no disk on which to resolve a symlink on the user's computer. destino/atalho -> /caminho/do/projeto passes through there unseen, and it is here that it is resolved.

A difference in mechanism, found while implementing: realpathMaisProximo falls back to the first ancestor that exists, and the mirror destination almost never exists (it is the mkdir -p of this round that creates it). Collapsing both sides onto the ancestor would make /base-outra and /base both become /, and the guard would refuse every sibling folder. That is why the second pass resolves the ancestor and puts the suffix back — a symlink can only live in a segment that exists, so what remains never hides any link. Refusal (1) also has a second half, per file (caminhoNoDestino): a destino/sub that links to /etc would make the copy of sub/passwd write outside, with the destination itself perfectly valid.

One direction, and it NEVER deletes. Workspace → destination. Never --delete, never unlink, never rm. A file deleted in the workspace remains in the destination, and that is a decision, not carelessness: the user's folder is not a replica, it is an accumulation — an agent that deletes a file in someone's personal folder because of a git clean on the other side is the surprise the product exists not to produce. Overwriting a file that changed is expected; removing never is. The price, declared in the ADR: the destination only grows, and no automatic mechanism cleans it.

What is copied is the GIT LIST, and nothing else. The tracked files (git ls-files) plus the untracked ones that are not ignored (git ls-files --others --exclude-standard), with -z (git quotes and escapes a path with a space or accent without it). That is exactly "the work": it skips node_modules, dist, build output and .git itself without keeping any exclusion list, which would age with every new stack — the project's .gitignore is already the list, maintained by whoever maintains the project. The workspace is a git repository by construction (the product provisions Gitflow in it and materializes it with git init/fetch/checkout), so the precondition belongs to the PRODUCT, not an assumption about the machine. Git that fails or a folder that is not a repository fail with a named reason — never a cp -r of everything as a plan B, which is how an entire node_modules would end up in someone's personal folder.

Two properties verified and declared, not hidden: a nested git repository comes back as ONE directory entry and is not descended into — the worktree of each dev agent (<workspace>/.worktrees/<agent_id>) is one of those, so the mirror shows the main checkout, never the work still isolated in a worktree; and a symlink at the source is skipped, because following the link would bring content from outside the project into the personal folder. What is left out is COUNTED (pulados/recusados), never swallowed. And there is no "did it change?" heuristic: always copying costs bytes that are already equal, while skipping by size+mtime would make the mirror silently not copy a file that changed.

Its OWN predicate, and the mirror does not require Docker. Engine.Runners.RunnerReadiness stays byte for byte as it is (ADR 0147, point 3) — Engine.Runners.Espelho does not call it, does not extend it and receives nothing from it. The mirror has TWO preconditions, confirmed workspace and connected runner, and not the third that RN-507 added (container REGISTERED running). A RunnerReadiness with a "skip container" flag is precisely the mechanism by which that third one would fall by accident for exec in a future refactoring, and ADR 0145 exists so that it does not fall. And the mirror legitimately does not need it: the third exists because there were two possible executions and the wrong one was invisible; a file copy on the user's machine has no container to fall from. It also does not ask for the execution_mode — whoever already decided that was the api when writing the destination (RN-515 refuses container), and repeating the decision would be the second source of the same rule.

Trigger by a NAMED MOMENT, never a watcher. The engine pushes mirror_sync from a point in the code that has a name — today the successful commit (EngineWeb.ActionCommandController, git_commit). Never fs.watch: a watcher is unbounded work triggered by anything — a dependency install, a build, and worse, by the mirror's own writes, which is a loop — and would run continuously on the user's machine without anyone having asked, which is the opposite of what "local agent" should mean. The push is fire-and-forget: no from, no pending_execs and no mirror_sync_result, because whoever triggered it is in the middle of something else and the sync telemetry is point 7 of the ADR, from another session. A mirror failure becomes a local log, never an exception that takes the runner down and never silence.

It is NOT a proposed_action, and must not become one. Writing the mirror is configuration the user declared, not an agent asking to act — ADR 0147 is explicit about it, and syncing via a terminal command would fall into the scope of ADR 0055 and become a queue of routine approvals, eroding the ceiling that gives the click its meaning.

The mirror state is visible, and the three states do not collapse (RN-517)​

RN-517 — The outcome of each mirror round comes back through the channel and becomes TELEMETRY in its own table; "never synced", "synced and copied nothing" and "failed" are THREE answers, and success and error coexist​

Session 8 of PHASE 28 and point 7 of ADR 0147. RN-516 made the mirror really copy and left mirror_sync fire-and-forget — with no mirror_sync_result in the protocol, on purpose, because the telemetry format was this delivery's decision. It is this one that closes the loop.

The path is that of workspace_confirm, and no other. The runner pushes mirror_sync_result on the terminal:<projectId> channel after the round ends; the engine handles it in handle_in/3 and RELAYS it to the api over internal HTTP (POST /internal/projects/:projectId/mirror-sync-result), which writes through the use case. The engine does not write the table — a second write path would be the second source of the same truth, and the first thing to diverge. It is the only precedent of the runner telling something about itself, and that is why the ADR named it.

Never an optimistic "ok". The reported outcome is the REAL one: the three counts that sincronizarEspelho returned (copied, skipped, refused — never recounted) or the named error. ALL THREE exits of tratarMirrorSync report, and with different messages: the refusal for a non-granted destination, the copy failure and the success. ok is NEVER deduced from there being a count or a message — neither in the runner, nor in the engine's translation, nor in the api's use case: deducing would make a round that copied 0 files (perfectly normal) indistinguishable from one that never even ran.

A TABLE, and not the event log. project_mirror_states, one row per project (unique project_id, same design as project_containers). The reason is the same one that made rag_searches become a table (RN-479): session_events.session_id is NOT NULL and a mirror round has no session — the event log would lose the whole thing, not part of it. And it is not a proposed_action under any circumstances: writing the mirror is configuration the user declared, not an agent asking to act.

The THREE states of RN-088, and they do not collapse. "Never synced" is the absent row. "Synced and copied nothing" is a present row with files_copied = 0 — an outcome, not an emptiness. "Failed" is last_error_at more recent than last_synced_at. They are three different answers, the person acts differently on each one, and a dash serving all three would be the screen refusing to name what it knows (RN-470).

Success and error COEXIST in the same row. The two writes mention disjoint columns: the success one does not touch last_error/last_error_at, the failure one does not touch any success column, and neither erases the other. What decides which one is CURRENT is the comparison of the two timestamps (deriveMirrorSyncStatus, a pure domain function), and that is what lets the screen say "the last round failed — last good copy yesterday, with 412 files". A destructive write of one side over the other would throw away precisely the most useful information the screen has while the mirror is broken. Two smaller choices in the same direction: a failure WITHOUT a destination does not erase the destination of the last copy that worked, and an exact timestamp tie resolves to failed — between asserting that everything is fine and asserting that something failed, the safe assertion is the one that makes the person look.

destination is FROZEN, like image_version in project_containers and the weights in rag_searches (RN-479): it is the REAL destination of that round, resolved by realpath on the user's machine after the mkdir -p. Reading projects.mirror_path at display time would state the destination of NOW over a copy from yesterday — and the two really diverge, because the grant travels in the join and only changes when the runner reconnects (RN-516). When they diverge, the screen SAYS so.

Writing telemetry never takes down what it measures. The copy has already finished when the report goes out; the engine's handle_in only LOGS the api's refusal and returns {:noreply, socket} in both branches, and the runner's channel stays alive. Without a channel (the connection dropped between the request and the end of the copy) the runner does not report and does not throw — the round that happened is not undone because of that. And a project whose destination was CLEARED midway still records: the round happened, and its error is what usually explains what happened.

On the screen, the row goes into AmbienteDoProjeto (the side column of the Overview, next to those of execution mode and runner) and only exists in a project that has mirrorPath — in a project without a mirror, "never synced" would be an invented absence, the same argument that already held for the runner row. An ABSOLUTE date with a caveat and never a green "it's up" dot, by the same precedent as workspaceVerifiedAt: the timestamp says a round happened, not that the folder is up to date with what changed afterwards (the trigger is a named moment, the commit — never a watcher). The status arrives RESOLVED from the api: the rule deciding which timestamp counts has a single source, and it is what decides which of the three sentences the person reads.

viewer role to READ, maintainer to write the destination — the rule of RN-102 applied: the minimum belongs to the ENDPOINT, and this one only reads. The destination already travels in every project read (GET /projects/:projectId, viewer), so requiring maintainer here would lock information away from whoever already sees it in the same project, which is the worse of the two defects because it is invisible to whoever lost the capability.
